read.sections.0.text.back: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk in Mesopotamia, which is Iraq today. Other early cities grew up on the banks of the Nile River in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some also grew up in the valley of the Yellow River in China. Later, cities also grew up in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a surplus of food. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then, many people could specialise in one type of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain allowed potters, builders and record keepers each to do one main job.
read.sections.0.text.source: More than 5,000 years ago, some farming towns grew into the first cities. One of the earliest was Uruk, in Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Other early cities grew beside the Nile in Egypt and the Indus River in South Asia. Some grew in the Yellow River valley in China. Later, cities also grew in Mexico, Central America and West Africa. Every city needed a food surplus. With extra food, thousands of people could eat without farming. Then many people could specialise in one kind of work. They became builders, potters, traders or priests. In Banwa, extra grain lets potters, builders and record keepers each do one main job.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk, in present-day Iraq, is one of the first. Other cities grew beside big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities grew in the American continent and West Africa. Cities needed a surplus, that is, extra food. So many people did not need to farm. They could specialise in one job. Some built, some traded. In Banwa, extra grain allowed people to do one main job.
read.sections.0.simpler.source: More than 5,000 years ago, the first cities began. Uruk, in what is now Iraq, was one of the first. Other cities grew by big rivers in Egypt, South Asia and China. Later, cities grew in the Americas and West Africa. A city needs a surplus, or extra food. Then many people do not need to farm. They can specialise. Some build, and some trade. In Banwa, extra grain lets people do one main job.

read.sections.1.heading.back: States have rulers, laws and taxes
read.sections.1.heading.source: States had rulers, laws and taxes

read.sections.1.text.back: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made decisions for everyone and settled disagreements. They also made laws, that is, rules that everyone must obey. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States also collected taxes, and people often paid them with grain, animals or labour. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, the leaders managed the building of canals and made rules about water.
read.sections.1.text.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is a group of people in one area who are led by one government. Rulers and officials made choices for everyone and settled arguments. They also made laws, which are rules that everyone must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi had about 280 laws carved on a tall black stone. States collected taxes too, and people often paid in grain, animals or work. In Egypt, farmers gave part of their harvest to the ruler. Taxes paid for canals, walls, storehouses and temples. In Banwa, leaders organise a canal and make rules about the water.

read.sections.1.simpler.back: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area that has one government. Its leaders make laws. Laws are rules that everyone must obey. In Babylon, King Hammurabi put his laws on a big stone. People also paid taxes, usually with grain or labour. That tax was used to build walls and canals. In Banwa, the leaders planned canals and made water rules.
read.sections.1.simpler.source: Many cities became part of a state. A state is an area with one government. Its leaders make laws. A law is a rule that all people must follow. In Babylon, King Hammurabi put his laws on a big stone. People also paid a tax, often in grain or work. The tax paid for walls and canals. In Banwa, the leaders plan a canal and make water rules.

read.sections.2.heading.back: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally
read.sections.2.heading.source: Writing helped, but power was not shared equally

read.sections.2.text.back: To collect taxes and divide up food, officials needed to note down many things. So some early states began to keep records in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya people in Central America also created their own writing. Indus cities also had writing marks, but no one has yet been able to read them. By working together, a city could build something that one family could not build. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected ordinary people, but others helped the powerful more.
read.sections.2.text.source: To collect taxes and share out food, officials needed to keep track of a lot. So some early states began to keep a record in writing. In Mesopotamia, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain and animals. Egypt, China and the Maya of Central America also made their own writing. The Indus cities had signs too, but nobody can read them yet. Working together, a city could build things that one family could not. But power was not shared equally. Rulers, officials and rich families often controlled land, grain and water. Some laws protected people, but others helped the powerful more.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Leaders needed to count a lot of grain. So some states began to keep records in writing. In present-day Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Egypt, China and the Maya people also created writing. No one has yet been able to read the Indus marks. In cities, people could build big things together. But power was not shared fairly. Rulers and rich families often had more land and grain. Some laws helped rich people more.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: Leaders needed to count lots of grain. So some states started to keep a record in writing. In what is now Iraq, people pressed marks into wet clay to count grain. Rulers and rich families often have more land and grain. Some laws help the rich more.

watch.summary.back: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the early states in the world. The Nile River flows through a dry desert. Every year, the river flooded and left fertile soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow a lot of grain. That surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile River was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods upstream and downstream. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This allowed Egypt to build very large projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
watch.summary.source: This video tells the story of ancient Egypt, one of the world's early states. The Nile River runs through a dry desert. Each year, the river flooded and left rich soil on its banks. Farmers used this soil to grow large amounts of grain. The surplus fed many people who did other work, such as builders, craftspeople and scribes, who wrote records. The Nile was also like a road. Boats carried food, stone and other goods up and down the river. Egypt was ruled by kings called pharaohs, with many officials to help them. They collected taxes, planned work and kept records. This let Egypt build huge projects. But power was not shared equally. Egypt is only one example. Other early cities and states grew in different ways.
